## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahāmorajātaka* (Ja 491) is a narrative in the Pali Jātaka collection, rendered into English as *The Golden Peacock* [SuttaCentral]. Its framing story is set at Jetavana, where the Buddha addresses a backsliding monk (*ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu*) confounded by lust for pleasure, remarking that the hurricane of passion has overwhelmed holy beings who had held aloof from desire for thousands of years [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1887]. In the story of the past, set during the reign of King Brahmadatta of Benares, the Bodhisatta was born from a golden egg as a marvelous golden peachick [Sujato 2011]. At the end of the narrative, following the revelation of the Four Noble Truths, the monk attains arahantship, and the Buddha identifies himself as the peacock king (*morarājā*) [Fausböll 1887].

Modern scholarship describes the tale as a prime example of an exalted quest for a mythical animal where compassion is the means of success [Sujato 2011]. Scholarly discussion also observes that the prose commentary mentions snakes among the perils from which the peacock remains free, comparing the figure of the peacock-king to related narratives such as the Suvarṇāvabhāsa account in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya [Schmithausen, Maitri magic]. Text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus reflects 21 matching passages (3,883 characters) shared with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Catuttho bhāgo), while no cross-language matches are registered in the automated corpus [DharmaNexus].
